source: issue #5 (explanation quoted from the live run; options reconstructed)
prompt: The change replaces a hand-written match with `?` when reading the config. What makes `?` compile in a function returning `Result<Config, ConfigError>`?
options: ConfigError implements From<io::Error>
io::Error has an inherent into_config_error method
ConfigError implements From<&str>
The function is marked #[must_use]
feedback: `?` calls From::from on the error, so ConfigError needs a From<io::Error> impl. Having an inherent function with a similar name or an `Err` type that implements `Display` does not satisfy the trait bound, and `From<&str>` is for infallible conversions from string slices, not for io errors.

prompt: The change replaces a hand-written match with `?` when reading the config. What makes `?` compile in a function returning `Result<Config, ConfigError>`?
options: ConfigError implements From<io::Error>
io::Error has an inherent into_config_error method
ConfigError implements From<&str>
The function is marked #[must_use]
feedback: An inherent method is never called by `?`. `?` calls From::from on the error, so ConfigError needs a From<io::Error> impl; a From<&str> impl converts string slices, not io errors, and #[must_use] only affects warnings.

prompt: Why does the change release the std Mutex guard before awaiting the fetch?
options: The guard is not Send, and holding it blocks other tasks on the lock
Mutex::lock panics if called inside an async function
The fetch needs mutable access to the cache entries
feedback: A std MutexGuard is not Send and keeps the lock held for the whole await, so other tasks block on it. Switching to an RwLock would not help either, since its write guard has the same problem.

prompt: Why does the change release the std Mutex guard before awaiting the fetch?
options: The guard is not Send, and holding it blocks other tasks on the lock
Mutex::lock panics if called inside an async function
The fetch needs mutable access to the cache entries
feedback: Locking a std Mutex inside an async function is allowed; it only blocks the thread while held. A std MutexGuard is not Send and keeps the lock held for the whole await, so other tasks on the worker block on it; dropping it first avoids both.

prompt: What goes wrong with `recipients=[]` as a default argument?
options: The same list is shared by every call that uses the default
Python rejects lists as default values
The list is garbage collected after the first call
feedback: Default values are evaluated once, when the function is defined, so every call without recipients appends to the same list. Calling list.copy() inside the function, as some suggest, would also work but is easy to forget.

prompt: What goes wrong with `recipients=[]` as a default argument?
options: The same list is shared by every call that uses the default
Python rejects lists as default values
The list is garbage collected after the first call
feedback: Default values are evaluated once, when the function is defined, so every call without recipients appends to the same list and later calls send mail to earlier users. Using None and creating the list in the body gives each call its own list.

prompt: What does replacing three sequential awaits with Promise.all change?
options: The requests run concurrently and the call fails as soon as one fails
The requests run on separate threads
The results come back in the order the requests finish
feedback: Running them at the same time, rather than one after another, is the point: total latency becomes the slowest request instead of the sum, and Promise.all rejects on the first failure. It is still one thread, and the results keep the order of the input array.

prompt: What does replacing three sequential awaits with Promise.all change?
options: The requests run concurrently and the call fails as soon as one fails
The requests run on separate threads
The results come back in the order the requests finish
feedback: The requests run concurrently on one thread and Promise.all rejects on the first failure. Promise.allSettled is wrong here because it would wait for every request and hide the failure from the caller.
